Title: Special Sessions - Emerging Scope and Design Challenges for Approximate Computing: Optimizing Accuracy-PPA trade-offs and Beyond
Text:
Special Sessions - Emerging Scope and Design Challenges for Approximate
Computing: Optimizing Accuracy-PPA trade-offs and Beyond
Siva Satyendra Sahoo1, Bastien Deveautour2, Marcello Traiola3, Chongyan Gu4, Yun Wu4, Aditya
Japa5, Salim Ullah6, Akash Kumar6
IMEC, Leuven, Belgium1, Nantes Université, CNRS, Nantes, France2, Univ Rennes, CNRS, Inria, Rennes, France3,
Queen’s University Belfast, U.K.4, Ulster University, Derry, U.K.5, Ruhr-Universität Bochum, Germany6
siva.satyendra.sahoo@imec.be,bastien.deveautour@univ-nantes.fr,marcello.traiola@inria.fr
{c.gu,yun.wu}@qub.ac.uk,a.japa@ulster.ac.uk,{salim.ullah,akash.kumar}@rub.de
Abstract
The rapid growth of AI workloads is driving interest in Approximate
Computing (AxC) as a means to enable low-cost, energy-efficient in-
ference in resource-constrained systems. By introducing controlled
inaccuracies, AxC can deliver substantial gains in power, perfor-
mance, and area (PPA) while leveraging the inherent error tolerance
of many AI models. Achieving this potential requires adapting ex-
isting frameworks to support the design and optimization of neural
networks with approximate operators. Modern AxC research ex-
tends beyond accuracy–PPA trade-offs to address reliability and
security, reducing redundancy overheads and exploring the distinc-
tive side-channel implications of approximation. Application-aware
approaches, such as those for spiking neural networks, show that
tailoring approximation to workload-specific error behavior can
surpass generic strategies. This article examines AI-guided design
methods and the interplay between efficiency, reliability, and se-
curity, highlighting how these interconnected facets can advance
embedded and high-performance computing.

Introduction
Modern Edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) platforms face stringent
Power-Performance-Area (PPA) constraints, challenging traditional
accuracy-first design strategies. While techniques such as quan-
tization, precision scaling, and voltage-frequency tuning aim to
reduce cost through conservative system-level margins, they often
preserve functional exactness and leave significant optimization
potential untapped. Approximate Computing (AxC) offers a more
aggressive alternative by relaxing computational exactness itself,

enabling disproportionate improvements in PPA. Although origi-
nally explored for energy-efficiency, AxC holds potential to mature
into a broader design paradigm for AI and signal-processing work-
loads, where bounded inaccuracy can be exploited for system-level
efficiency. As illustrated in Fig. 1, increasing approximation allows
for lower PPA cost, defining a trade-off frontier between efficiency
and error. Yet this frontier is not static—its shape and extent de-
pend heavily on how approximation is applied. Emerging direc-
tions—spanning application-aware design, AI-driven exploration,
reliability co-design, and security-aware approximation—actively
reshape and extend this frontier, unlocking new regions of the de-
sign space beyond what traditional optimization techniques allow
us to explore.
To fully exploit the AxC design space, it is essential to move
beyond one-size-fits-all operator libraries and embrace methods tai-
lored to application structure and workload-level error resilience. As
highlighted by the ACC-DRIVEN DESIGN and AI-DRIVEN SEARCH
arrows in Fig. 1, application-aware design (Section 5) adapts Ap-
proximate Operators (AxOs) to domain-specific tolerance, shifting
the frontier leftward by reducing required error for a given PPA
cost. Complementing this, AI-guided exploration (Section 2) uses
learning-based models and evolutionary heuristics to efficiently
navigate the vast space of candidate designs, pushing the frontier
downward by identifying more efficient solutions. Together, these
approaches expand the trade-off space more intelligently than tra-
ditional heuristics, yielding designs better aligned with both system
constraints and algorithmic robustness.
While AxC offers compelling efficiency gains, its impact on sys-
tem dependability and trust must be carefully considered. As shown
in Fig. 1, reliability constraints (Section 3) limit how far AxC can
push PPA savings by bounding approximation to maintain/improve
fault tolerance—especially in safety-critical or long-lifetime deploy-
ments. At the same time, AxC introduces new security dynamics

2
AI-driven Optimization of Accuracy-PPA
Trade-offs
2.1
Approximation through Logic Pruning
A key strategy in approximate computing involves pruning re-
dundant or less critical logic elements within arithmetic opera-
tors, significantly simplifying computational structures [2]. Logic
pruning aims to reduce gate-level complexity by identifying logic
paths or components whose contribution to output accuracy is
minimal, enabling power and area savings with bounded error
overhead. Techniques for pruning include structural analysis [2],
simulation-based sensitivity tracking [3], and functional signifi-
cance heuristics [4], which assess the impact of removing gates
or signals on output fidelity. By aggressively reducing the inter-
nal logic of operators, pruning can reduce switching activity, logic
depth, and overall footprint. However, ensuring that such reduc-
tions stay within acceptable application-level accuracy margins
remains a challenge, especially for datapaths reused across multiple
contexts. Prior research, including methods like EvoApprox [5],
has explored evolutionary heuristics to automatically explore this
pruning space for logic circuits such as adders and multipliers.
Among these approaches, Lookup Table (LUT)-based pruning has
emerged as particularly well-suited to Field Programmable Gate
Array (FPGA) architectures due to its direct mapping onto fabric
resources [2].
FPGAs, relying heavily on LUTs for logic implementation, pro-
vide unique opportunities for resource-aware pruning at the opera-
tor level. LUTs implement Boolean functions using configuration
bits, with input-output mappings hardcoded in SRAM-based truth
tables. As illustrated in Fig. 2, pruning the LUT configuration in-
volves selectively invalidating low-impact input combinations (e.g.,
setting outputs to zero) or collapsing multiple entries to reduce
switching or eliminate entire LUTs. These changes directly reduce
dynamic power and logic usage. For example, suppose analysis
shows certain inputs (e.g., input 6) have a negligible effect on out-
put precision in specific contexts. In that case, these paths can be
truncated to simplify the LUT usage without significant loss in
accuracy. The annotated figure shows such a case, where entries

design spaces with precision and architectural alignment.
2.2
Search Space for Approximate Operators
Traditional selection-based AxO design methodologies utilize
fixed approximate operators from limited libraries, inherently re-
stricting achievable design optimizations. This is particularly ev-
ident in convolution-based workloads such as Conv2D, where a
single layer may invoke multiple instances of arithmetic operations
like multiplication. As shown in Fig. 3(a), selecting AxOs from a
small library (e.g., 13 pre-designed 8-bit multipliers from EvoAp-
prox) provides only a constrained set of trade-offs across each kernel
element, limiting the granularity of approximation across spatial
dimensions. In a typical 3 × 3 convolution kernel, this results in
a fairly large, combinatorial space of 139 possible operator-level
mappings – a large design space, yet often insufficient to reach
Pareto-optimal designs for specific accuracy-PPA trade-offs. As
kernel sizes or operator widths increase, the combinatorial space
becomes both under-explored and suboptimal. Furthermore, fixed
AxOs often lack tunability to application-specific constraints, lead-
ing to either over-conservative or excessively error-prone choices.
Given these limitations, synthesis approaches that dynamically
generate AxOs tailored to an application become necessary for a
comprehensive exploration of the approximation space.
In contrast to selection methods, synthesis approaches dynami-
cally generate approximate operators tailored explicitly to application-
specific constraints, enabling deeper optimization of both accuracy
and PPA. These approaches allow for fine-grained pruning of logic
or LUT resources—capturing a broader spectrum of approximate
behaviors not available in pre-built libraries. For example, as shown
in Fig. 3(a), synthesizing a Conv2D kernel with 9 independently
tunable AxOs can expose vast new design points, each represented
by a unique combination of logic pruning or configuration bits.
However, this flexibility introduces a significant increase in search
complexity: even for moderately sized kernels and operand widths,

the design space becomes intractably large for brute-force evalua-
tion. Managing this synthesis-based space necessitates intelligent
Design Space Exploration (DSE) strategies. This motivates the use of
metaheuristic search methods like evolutionary algorithms, Monte
Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), etc., which iteratively evolve candidate
solutions using population-based search, or random simulations –
efficiently identifying high-quality approximate designs that meet
both PPA and error bounds.
2.3
DSE for Approximate Operators
Genetic Algorithms (GA) are commonly employed in AxO opti-
mization due to their robustness and flexibility in navigating com-
plex design spaces [1, 6, 7]. GA-based DSE frameworks explore
operator configurations by evolving a population of candidate de-
signs, each represented using binary-encoded LUT usage patterns
(as shown in Fig. 4(a)). Through cycles of selection, crossover, and mu-
tation, new generations of approximate operators are synthesized
and evaluated to optimize PPA, and behavioral accuracy (BEHAV)
metrics. However, the effectiveness of GA is often constrained by
the significant computational overhead involved in evaluating each
design candidate. This is particularly prominent in operator-rich
workloads where the fitness evaluation—comprising logic synthesis,
power/timing analysis, and behavioral accuracy estimation—must
be repeated for hundreds or thousands of candidates per generation.
Prior efforts, such as AppAxO [1] and AxOTreeS [4], highlight this
bottleneck, where exhaustive evaluations limit the scalability of
the DSE process. As shown in Fig. 4(b), the BEHAV estimation can
also increase significantly depending upon the size of the applica-
tion’s dataset. To mitigate these computational overheads, Machine
Learning (ML)-based surrogate models have emerged as an essential
adaptation strategy and form part of tools such as AxOSyn [8].
Incorporating ML surrogate models into GA-based exploration
significantly accelerates the optimization process. Surrogate models
approximate expensive evaluation metrics—such as PPA and BE-
HAV–with high fidelity and minimal computational cost, enabling
rapid assessment of large candidate populations. As illustrated
in Fig. 4(a), once a sufficiently accurate surrogate is trained, it re-
places full evaluations for most candidates during the evolutionary
search, reserving only a small subset for ground-truth validation.

Techniques like AppAxO [1] and AxOMaP [6] have demonstrated

By providing low-cost, accurate predictions, surrogate models al-

2.4
Advanced AI/ML-based DSE
While traditional surrogate methods effectively accelerate DSE,
advanced AI/ML techniques enable deeper insights into AxO be-
havior. Conventional regression-based surrogates often function as
black-box estimators, offering limited interpretability and inflex-
ible adaptation to varying search dynamics. In contrast, modern
AI/ML strategies enable a richer characterization of the design
space, providing actionable insights into feature impact, operator
structure, and the application’s behavioral patterns. For instance,
as shown in Fig. 5(a), AI/ML plays multiple roles beyond a fast
surrogate. First, it generates candidates: SyFAxO-GeN [9] trains
constraint-aware Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that
directly emit LUT-level FPGA implementations of approximate
multipliers, then uses learned estimators to rank them—improving
Pareto coverage and reporting up to 49% faster GAN training with
negligible accuracy loss versus related generators. This shifts ML
from “predictor” to producer in the loop. Second, ML analyzes char-
acterization data to reveal structure (e.g., LUT usage correlations)
and then adapts the optimizer. AxOMaP [6] converts such statis-
tics into MIQCP formulations whose solutions warm-start/prune
evolutionary search. AxOCS [7] exploits cross–bit-width regulari-
ties to supersample larger operators from smaller ones, providing
informed seeds before refinement. Together, these steps realize the
flow shown in Fig. 5(a).
Fig. 5(b)-(c) illustrate two concrete, complementary search con-
trollers. For GA-based flows (Fig. 5(b)), AI/ML augmentation im-
proves both convergence speed and final quality: AxOMaP reports
up to 21% hypervolume gain over GA-only by MIQCP-guided seed-
ing/filtering, while AxOCS uses ML-based supersampling to trans-
fer patterns from 8-bit to larger designs and deliver stronger ini-
tial populations for multi-objective search. For tree-based flows


(Fig. 5(c)), AxOTreeS [4] formulates synthesis as MCTS guided
by learned estimators and problem-specific statistics (e.g., LUT-
importance), pruning unpromising branches and focusing rollouts
where payoff is likely—achieving up to 1.6× hypervolume improve-
ment vs. vanilla MCTS on tight constraints.
3
Balancing Efficiency and Reliability: the Role
of Approximate Computing
3.1
Motivation and Concepts
Efficiency and reliability are often opposing goals, especially in
resource-constrained safety-critical systems, where failures are un-
acceptable. Designers seek minimal energy, area, and latency, while
reliability typically requires spatial, temporal, or data redundancy.
Striking the right balance is challenging, particularly in modern
neural network (NN) and edge-computing deployments.
AxC improves efficiency by relaxing exactness, deliberately in-
troducing small errors to reduce energy, latency, and area—from
circuit-level units to algorithms. This trade-off is acceptable in inher-
ently error-resilient domains such as multimedia, machine learning,
and NNs, where minor perturbations rarely harm performance.
Beyond efficiency, AxC can enhance resilience by leveraging the
natural fault tolerance of some workloads. When combined with
techniques like fault-aware training or precision-aware design, it
can enable graceful degradation and adaptive responses. While
approximation may reduce redundancy and increase vulnerability,
research shows that faults and approximations can sometimes mask
each other’s effects. This has led to Approximation for Reliability,
where approximation is used to maintain or even improve fault
tolerance alongside efficiency gains [10–12].
In the following, we review both general-purpose and domain-
specific AxC-based fault-tolerance methods at design-time and run-
time, showing how AxC can serve as both a performance booster
and a reliability-driven design philosophy.
3.2
General-purpose AxC application for
fault-tolerance
Conventional fault-tolerant architectures, such as Triple Modular
Redundancy (TMR), replicate functional modules and use majority
voting to mask faults. While effective, TMR’s area, energy, and per-
formance penalties often make it unsuitable for resource-limited
systems. Approximate Triple Modular Redundancy (ATMR) reduces
these costs by replacing some or all redundant modules with approx-
imate hardware, such as low-power multipliers or adders, while
still preserving fault-masking capability. This design-time approach
exploits the intrinsic error resilience of workloads such as neural
networks, where small deviations in computation are negligible
compared to the effects of real faults. The result is a practical balance
between fault resilience and resource efficiency [13].
The Quadruple Approximate Modular Redundancy (QAMR) con-
cept extends this idea with a four-module arrangement. Each mod-
ule is intentionally simplified via approximation, which reduces
costs. However, the four modules are co-approximated so that for
any given output and input, at least three replicas produce the pre-
cise value, ensuring single fault masking, exactly like in TMR. By
reducing the per-module cost enough, the four approximated mod-
ules can take less area, delay, and power than three precise modules.
The net result is full TMR-level reliability at a lower cost [14–17].
Compared to ATMR, QAMR improves fault coverage while still
operating with fewer resources than TMR. These methods illus-
trate how design-time AxC can significantly reduce overhead while
maintaining high resilience.
Beyond design-time strategies, AxC can enable runtime adapta-
tion of fault tolerance. The hybrid architecture in [18] shows how
reconfigurable modules can handle transient and permanent faults
by switching between logic blocks. While originally implemented
with three accurate combinational logic (CL) blocks, this concept
could be expanded by including approximate modules—similar to
ATMR—within the reconfiguration pool. The system could then
adjust both redundancy and approximation level on the fly: in
low-criticality or energy-constrained modes, approximate replicas
could be selected to save power; in safety-critical scenarios, accu-
rate replicas could be activated for maximum fault coverage. Such
runtime flexibility, when combined with AxC, provides a scalable
means to balance performance, energy, and reliability across diverse
operating conditions.
3.3
Domain-specific AxC application for
fault-tolerance
In this subsection, we explore how domain-specific considera-
tions shape the use of AxC for fault tolerance. While the principles
apply across many domains, we illustrate them through Deep Neu-
ral Networks (DNNs), a class of workloads widely deployed on spe-
cialized hardware in edge, embedded, and safety-critical systems.
DNNs’ high computational demands and constrained deployment
environments make them promising candidates for AxC to improve
efficiency. However, the interplay between approximation and re-
liability in such critical settings demands careful, domain-aware
design. Although DNNs have some inherent fault resilience due
to statistical behavior and architectural redundancy, hardware for
DNNs (HW-DNN) remains vulnerable to faults from manufactur-
ing defects, silicon aging, and environmental stress such as heat or
ionizing radiation. These faults can cause operational failures with
serious consequences in critical applications. As motivated in the
previous section, conventional fault tolerance methods like TMR
and Error Correcting Codes (ECCs) are effective in general com-
puting but must be adapted to HW-DNNs to remain cost-effective.
A notable design-time solution is the Fault-Aware Training (FAT)
framework [19], which improves DNN robustness by injecting hard-
ware fault models into the training process. This allows the network
to learn weights that are inherently more resilient to errors caused
by approximate or faulty hardware during inference. By anticipat-
ing hardware unreliability during training, FAT produces models
that require no additional redundancy or protection mechanisms
at inference time, thereby offering a cost-effective and hardware-
aware approach to enhancing reliability.
Another design-time solution is proposed by Wei et al. in [20],
where AxC is combined with selective redundancy to create a fault-
tolerant Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) accelerator. Their
method leverages approximate arithmetic units, such as multipliers
and adders, in error-resilient parts of the network while preserv-
ing accuracy in more critical sections through selective duplica-
tion and checking. The design includes integrated error detection
mechanisms to handle transient or permanent faults, enabling a

In contrast to these design-time approaches, the AdAM archi-

for edge DNN accelerators. AdAM detects faults using leading-
one detection logic and dynamically selects between multiple ap-

required inference quality. This run-time adaptation allows the
system to gracefully degrade precision in the presence of hardware
errors, maintaining functional output, and conserving resources.
By embedding AxC into a dynamic fault response, AdAM provides
a flexible and efficient way to ensure reliable DNN execution in
power-constrained or fault-prone environments.
3.4
Quantitative Results
To showcase the impact of AxC on fault tolerance in CNNs,
we refer to the study conducted in [22], which investigates how
different Approximate Multipliers affect the resilience of a CNN
accelerator based on systolic arrays under fault conditions. The
evaluation uses the LeNet-5 NN architecture trained on the MNIST
dataset. The network consists of two convolutional layers, two fully
connected layers, and a softmax output layer. Importantly, the net-
work is trained without approximation: all weights and activations
are computed using full-precision arithmetic during training. The
approximation is introduced only during inference to isolate its
effect on fault resilience. Inference is performed on a CNN acceler-
ator implemented using a systolic array architecture. The systolic
array is designed with a fixed 8-bit datapath and uses an output-
stationary dataflow, where each Processing Element (PE) includes
a multiplier and an adder. A total of 36 PEs (6×6 array) are used to
parallelize matrix multiplications. The baseline configuration uses
exact 8-bit multipliers.
To evaluate the impact of AxC, the exact multipliers in each PE
are replaced with an approximate multiplier of [5]. Five multipliers
were used, and are listed in Fig. 6(a). Each provides a different trade-
off between hardware cost and computational accuracy. These mul-
tipliers significantly reduce area, power, and delay, but introduce
increasing levels of error in their outputs. Note that the multipliers
are designed to operate on 12-bit values, and the authors only used
the least significant 8 bits, reducing the performance of the multi-
pliers. Hence, fault resilience is evaluated through a bit-level fault
injection campaign, using the framework described in [23]. Each
configuration reported in the table was evaluated under identical
fault scenarios. Results in Fig. 6(a) show the percentage of injected
faults that led to a specific outcome. In particular, we report three
outcomes: (i) fault does not impact the final outputs (we refer to
this class as masked), (ii) the fault impacts the final outputs but
does not change the CNN top-1 accuracy (we refer to this class
as benign), and (iii) the fault changes the CNN accuracy (we refer
to this class as critical). The general trend is that approximation
does not help or even worsens fault tolerance, i.e., fewer faults are
classified as masked and benign, and more lead to critical outcomes
w.r.t. the accurate version. However, for mul12s_34P we observe
a 10% absolute increase in masked faults w.r.t. the accurate mul-
tiplier and of about 4% in benign faults. As also highlighted for
the general-purpose case in Section 3.2, these results suggest that
under particular conditions, AxC offers the opportunity to improve
HW-DNN fault tolerance, and not just its efficiency.
Fig. 6(b) shows a focus on the mul12s_34P multiplier. It shows
details about the number of critical outcomes resulting from injec-
tions in different output bits of the multipliers (bit 1 = MSB, i.e.,
sign). The height of the bars shows the critical fault percentage
per injected bit position. The blue color indicates the percentage
of critical injections that modify bits from value 0 to 1, while yel-
low reports those modifying bits from value 1 to 0. The reported
values above the blue bars refer to the percentage of bitflips from
value 0 to 1. In general, results show that bitflips from 0 to 1 more
commonly cause critical faults (more than 90%). It indicates that
the network using this multiplier is especially sensitive to faults
that increase a value’s magnitude, rather than those that decrease it.
Moreover, fault injections in the three Least Significant Bits (LSBs)
rarely caused critical faults – less than 1% per bit – which is prob-
ably the reason for increased masked and benign faults observed
in Fig. 6(a). Similar observations can be used to drive the design of
low-cost AxC-based fault tolerance approaches.
This analysis shows that AxC, besides improving efficiency, can
enhance fault tolerance in CNN accelerators. In some cases, ap-
proximate multipliers reduce resource usage while also mitigating
hardware faults through inherent error masking. Future approx-
imate designs should explicitly target both efficiency and fault
tolerance, e.g., as in the AdAM architecture [21]. Furthermore, an
underexplored area is the dynamic or layer-specific approximations
for adaptive resilience tuning based on workload, energy, or relia-
bility needs. Moreover, despite AxC’s potential, there is a lack of
fine-grained reliability analysis for embedded FPGA-based DNN
accelerators. The FPGA fault injection framework in [24] allows
controlled emulation of soft errors, yet most evaluations focus on
global accuracy trends, ignoring spatial fault sensitivity within ar-
chitectures like systolic arrays. For example, an most-significant bit
(MSB) fault in a PE near the output may be far less harmful than
the same fault at the input stage, where it could propagate through
subsequent computations. This positional effect is especially rele-
vant in FPGAs, where resource distribution varies across the fabric.
Addressing these location-dependent impacts is essential for selec-
tive hardening in heterogeneous approximate DNNs. Future work
should integrate position-aware fault analysis and mitigation to
enable truly efficient and fault-resilient hardware accelerators for
DNNs tailored to both architecture and physical layout.


4
Hardware Security in/for Approximate
Computing
Several attacks discussed or demonstrated in the literature raise con-
cerns about Approximate Computing (AxC) [27, 28], e.g., malicious
modifications, incorrect DRAM refresh rates, and deanonymiza-
tion. Based on reported vulnerabilities, potential attacks, including
side-channel analysis (SCA), hardware Trojan insertion, reverse
engineering, and cloning, show a large impact on all applications
that use AxC-based systems. On the other hand, AxC is also be-
ing explored to enhance the security of computational systems.
Several security solutions exploiting approximate systems, such as
information hiding, homomorphic encryption, and authentication,
have been successfully demonstrated with the additional benefit of
saving resources [28].
4.1
Hardware Security
Physical Unclonable Functions Physical unclonable function (PUF)
uses manufacturing process variations to generate an unclonable
digital fingerprint [29]. PUFs have been explored for several appli-
cations, including secret key generation, device identification, and
authentication. Depending on additional hardware utilization, PUFs
can be categorized into intrinsic PUFs and non-intrinsic PUFs [29].
Intrinsic PUFs, e.g., processor PUFs, utilize existing hardware [30]
to generate the response. An overclocking-based processor PUF,
scan-chain-based PUF, and a dynamic timing-aware processor PUF
have been proposed recently [31, 32]. However, these PUF designs
show poor uniqueness, require several design constraints, and cause
an increase in power consumption.
Side Channel Analysis Among the wide variety of physical at-
tacks introduced, SCA attacks have proved to be simple and effective
in recovering secret information [33]. These attacks are applied
to cryptographic engines to retrieve the original key information.
SCA is mainly classified into power analysis, Electromagnetic (EM)
signal analysis, and photonic analysis [34, 35]. Recently, SCAs have
been demonstrated against neural network accelerators to retrieve
weights, structure, and parameters of the network [36, 37]. The
process of conducting SCAs can be simplified by the inherently
lightweight nature of AxC-based systems, which often involve re-
duced hardware complexity and smaller computational footprints.
Conversely, the intrinsic error characteristics introduced by ap-
proximation can complicate the execution and analysis of such
attacks, introducing unpredictable variations in side-channel leak-
age. This dual effect underscores the need for further research to
fully understand and address the security implications of AxC.
4.2
PUF Design for Approximate Computing
This section presents the benefits and utility of AxC towards
intrinsic processor PUF. The performance and metrics of PUF are
analyzed to identify the benefits for AxC. Several dedicated PUF
designs include ring oscillator PUFs, arbiter PUFs, and flip-flop-
based PUFs, which utilize dedicated hardware and show large area
and energy consumption overheads [29, 30, 39]. Intrinsic proces-
sor PUFs leveraging AxC techniques have been explored due to
their minimal additional hardware requirements and strong suit-
ability for securing AxC-based systems. The first PUF to exploit
this concept measured instruction failures induced by overclocking
a microprocessor pipeline [31]. While innovative, this approach
suffers from poor uniqueness, is constrained by multiple design
limitations, and requires numerous repeated instruction executions
to reliably estimate the error rate. Moreover, the overclocking pro-
cess increases power consumption, leading to a considerable power
overhead. A dynamic timing-aware processor PUF has been demon-
strated that utilizes the floating-point unit of a processor with much
lower power consumption [32]. However, the uniqueness of the re-
sulting PUF is very poor. More recently, a widely adopted AxC tech-
nique—voltage scaling—has been applied to processor datapaths
to elicit PUF characteristics [25, 26]. In this approach, a general-
purpose processor datapath subjected to supply voltage scaling
leverages dominant chip-to-chip delay variations to reveal unique
device signatures. Using this method, researchers have demon-
strated a PUF design in which the extracted bits from the processor
datapath under reduced supply voltage exhibit significantly higher
uniqueness compared to earlier approaches.
A systematic voltage scaling is applied on the processor datap-
ath (as shown in Fig. 7(a)) to obtain the behaviour of PUF. With
a fixed clock period (𝑇𝐶𝐿𝐾) of 2𝑛𝑠(500MHz), for any sub-nominal
voltage (from 0.75V to 0.5V), the design demonstrates negative slack
(due to the increased delay), the design exhibits timing errors, and
operates in an AxC region. The design samples exhibit a variable
average error for 500 inputs and a population of 20 devices. This
demonstrates the distinct inter-die difference in failure behavior
even averaged over a set of inputs with chip-to-chip variations,
as shown in Fig. 7(b). PUF metrics, including uniqueness and re-
liability, are calculated by varying the supply voltages as shown
in Fig. 7(c). It is observed that the uniqueness of the PUF increases
with the reduction in supply voltage, and this region is highly suit-
able for PUF. In contrast, the reliability of PUFs is reduced with a
reduction in supply voltage. However, the optimum uniqueness and
reliability are identified for better operation of the PUF. Moreover,
depending on the application, the designer can choose the supply
voltage that can provide the required uniqueness and reliability.
In contrast to dedicated PUF designs, AxC provides several new
features to processor designs that can be utilized to improve re-
source optimization for PUF design. However, more research in
this direction is required to reap the full benefits of AxC to support
lightweight security strategies.
4.3
SCA of Approximate Computing
The growing global demand for high-performance computing
has driven the energy consumption of data centers and compute
clusters to unprecedented levels in recent years [40]. A major con-
tributor to this trend is the rapid proliferation of computation-
ally intensive Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs)-based AI applica-
tions [41]. As discussed earlier, AxC—also referred to as transparent
or inexact computing—has emerged as a promising strategy for re-
ducing energy consumption by relaxing exactness requirements
in error-tolerant workloads. Given their inherent resilience to mi-
nor computational errors, ANNs represent a natural fit for such
techniques, making approximate ANNs (AANNs) a likely candidate
for future edge deployments where energy budgets are especially
constrained. Recent studies have demonstrated that integrating
approximate circuits into the PEs of ANNs can yield substantial

savings in area, energy, and latency compared to exact implemen-
tations [42, 43]. However, as these systems increasingly operate in
security-critical environments, safeguarding their information pro-
cessing, model parameters, and architectural details from modern
SCAs has become imperative.
Side-channel attacks such as cache-timing, Electromigration
(EM), and power-based techniques have all been shown to extract
sensitive information from ANNs [36, 37]. Since approximation
inherently modifies the power and timing characteristics of the
hardware, it stands to reason that it will also influence the effective-
ness and detectability of such attacks—though the nature and extent
of this impact remain to be fully understood. In hardware terms,
each neuron in an ANN can be implemented as a PE that computes
a weighted sum. Understanding how approximation at this level
interacts with the leakage mechanisms exploited in SCAs is there-
fore a critical step toward designing secure and energy-efficient
approximate AI accelerators.
The objective is to evaluate the relative leakage of different ap-
proximate PEs (with voltage scaling, frequency scaling, and bitwise
approximation) based on the design proposed in [42], consisting
of two 4-bit multipliers and an 8-bit adder, as shown in Fig. 8(a).
Multiple versions of this PE were implemented at 45nm CMOS and
simulated using Cadence EDA tools with varying levels of bitwise
approximation from 0 bits (exact design) to 4 bits (50% approxima-
tion). For the power analysis attack, we use a Correlation Power
Analysis (CPA)-based approach, focusing on the multiply-add oper-
ation within the PE which is visualized in Fig. 8(b). Further, Fig. 8(c)
shows the measurement-to-disclosure (MTD) for each test case.
MTD is defined as the minimum number of power traces required
to retrieve the original weight information. To calculate this, the
attack was repeated using 256, 512, 768, and 1024 traces. The point
where the dotted line (original weight) becomes distinct from the
general body of potential weights is the MTD. In this test, the base-
line value is 48 for an exact PE. Voltage scaling increases this to 570
at 25% error, and above 1024 at 37% error. Frequency scaling like-
wise increases to roughly 600 at 25% error and somewhere above
1024 at 37% error. The bitwise approximation performs better than
the exact case but worse than other methods with an MTD of 200
at 25% error and roughly 512 at 37% error. The voltage scaling, fre-
quency scaling, and bitwise approximation obfuscated the power
traces’ information with inherent errors. Due to this, the power
traces may become noisy, MTD is increased, and it is harder for the
attacker to obtain secret weight information.

that intentionally relaxes output accuracy requirements in error-
resilient applications to reduce critical path delay (CPD), hardware

proposing approximation techniques across the computing stack
that trade accuracy for performance and efficiency [44–48]. Among
these techniques, AxO have received particular attention as a prac-
tical and effective solution for AI workload acceleration [49, 50].
This focus is motivated by the dominance of arithmetic operations—
especially Multiply-accumulate (MAC) units—across a wide range
of AI models and the inherent error tolerance of these applications.
For instance, as discussed in Section 2, a commonly used strategy
for AxO generation (circuit-level approximations) is the bottom-
up approach, which typically involves pruning a generic operator
model.
For example, Fig. 9(a) illustrates the design space of a signed
7-bit adder implemented using the AppAxO model [1]. As dis-
cussed in Section 2, unlike selection-based approaches that rely on
a pre-designed library of AxOs for application-level accuracy-PPA
trade-off exploration, frameworks such as AppAxO enable dynamic
generation of AxOs tailored to specific application requirements. In
this example, the accurate implementation—referred to as BASE —
uses seven 6-input LUTs to add two 7-bit inputs and generate a
7-bit output, which results in arithmetic overflows for certain input
combinations. To evaluate error-LUT trade-offs, its outputs are com-
pared against an overflow-safe reference adder that also processes
7-bit inputs but produces an 8-bit result. Fig. 9(b) illustrates the use
of the same AxOs as accumulators in a Spiking Neural Network
(SNN) for MNIST classification. The resulting Pareto front—based
on LUT utilization and classification error—shows a similar trend,
with five dominant designs that trade accuracy for resource (LUTs)
savings. In such AxO explorations, the highest application-level ac-
curacy is typically achieved by the accurate operator. For instance,
the BASE design, which utilizes 7 LUTs, yields the maximum classi-
fication accuracy i.e., the lowest classification error. However, since
the base operator (the generic implementation of the adder) was not
optimized for the specific computational patterns and requirements
of SNN operations, the potential for application-level accuracy im-
provements through such generic AxO exploration remains limited.
This conventional perspective of AxC raises an intriguing question:
Can AxC be leveraged not only to preserve computational efficiency
but also to enhance application-level accuracy beyond that of exact
computation—without incurring additional overhead in resources,
latency, or energy consumption?

Addressing this question necessitates a thorough exploration of
application-specific characteristics that can be leveraged to guide
the design of more effective approximations. This approach repre-
sents a shift in perspective, positioning AxC as not only a resource
optimization technique, but also a means to enhance accuracy in
targeted, resource-constrained scenarios. To address this intriguing
research question, a recent work, AxOSpike [51], considers SNNs as
a benchmark application, analyzing their operational characteristics
and leveraging these insights to guide the design of application-
aware AxOs. The goal is to achieve improved application-level
accuracy while maintaining PPA metrics comparable to those of
accurate operators. In the following, we discuss the SNN-specific
computational characteristics that have been analyzed to guide the
design of approximate operators capable of improving application-
level accuracy beyond that of accurate baseline implementations.
5.2
SNN Architectural Characteristics
In our work AxOSpike, we use a fully connected SNN for MNIST
digit classification. The network comprises an input layer, a single
hidden layer, and an output layer, and processes 28 × 28 grayscale
images. For our analysis, we adopt the basic Integrate-and-Fire
(IF) model, shown in Fig. 10, which excludes decay and refractory
mechanisms and uses membrane voltage as the sole internal state.
Furthermore, rate encoding is employed to translate input features
into spike frequencies. Neurons integrate weighted input spikes
over time and emit an output spike when the membrane voltage
exceeds a fixed threshold. The classification of the MNIST dataset
is based on spike counts at the output layer over 10 timesteps. This
simplified setup enables focused analysis of the impact of variations
in the accumulator operator.
As shown in Fig. 10, each SNN neuron contains an accumulator
referred to as a W×N_𝑁accumulator, where W ≤N. This accumu-
lator sums W-bit weights to generate an N-bit output. The output
bit width, N, is a crucial design parameter since it influences the
frequency of arithmetic overflows produced by the accumulator.
Assigning N = W can lead to frequent arithmetic overflows, which
occur when the addition of two positive values results in a negative
output, or two negative values produce a positive output due to

generates a spike when the accumulated sum of weighted input
spikes reaches a predefined threshold. However, due to overflow,
the accumulated value may wrap around—for example, a large pos-
itive sum may overflow into a negative value, or a large negative
sum may wrap toward a positive value—preventing the correct
threshold from being reached, as shown in Fig. 11. Although the
threshold itself influences accuracy, setting it too low or too high
can further degrade performance. To mitigate these effects, a larger
output bit width N in the W × N_𝑁accumulator can be used. How-
ever, FPGA-optimized implementations of W × N_𝑁and N × N_𝑁
adders exhibit comparable PPA characteristics.
To this end, we exploit approximation as a means to mitigate
arithmetic overflows in the BASE adder during accumulation. To
support proper accumulator behavior, including resetting to zero,
our proposed overflow-safe adder guarantees that operations of
the form 𝑋+ (−𝑋) always yield zero. The adder functions like a
conventional design (BASE adder) when the input operands have
opposite signs. However, when both operands share the same sign
(either positive or negative), it dynamically switches to an approxi-
mate mode, producing an output with the same sign as the inputs.
Although this output may be numerically imprecise, preserving
the sign helps prevent overflows in practice. Notably, the control
logic required to implement this behavior introduces no additional
resource overhead compared to the adder.
5.3
Overflow-safe Approximate Signed Adder
Fig. 13 presents the generalized architecture of the proposed
overflow-safe approximate adder, denoted as N × N_N AccMSB .
This architecture follows the LUT- and carry chain–based imple-
mentation described in Fig. 2. Unlike the baseline adder (in Fig. 2,
this design modifies the behavior of the two most significant LUTs
when both operands have the same sign. Specifically, the second
most significant LUT and its associated carry chain element al-
ways generate a carry-out of 0, which is propagated to the most
significant stage. This fixed carry-in is then used by the most sig-
nificant LUT and its carry chain to compute the sign bit of the
output. As a result, the output bit 𝑆𝑁−2 becomes approximate un-
der same-sign input conditions. This approximation ensures that
the output retains the input sign, effectively preventing arithmetic
overflows. Furthermore, AxOSpike supports logic pruning similar
to AppAxO, which typically replaces pruned computational blocks
with a constant zero (Fig. 2). In contrast, AxOSpike extends this
strategy by allowing pruned blocks to be replaced with either ‘0’
or ‘1’. This additional flexibility expands the AxO design space and
can significantly improve output accuracy in certain scenarios.

5.4
Quantitative Results
Fig. 13 compares the MNIST classification accuracy using BASE and
AccMSB adders as accumulators in the SNN’s neurons across differ-
ent threshold values. The AccMSB design consistently outperforms
BASE design across a wide range of threshold values, demonstrating
improved accuracy due to its ability to mitigate overflow-induced
errors through sign-preserving approximation. Fig. 14 compares
the SNN application-level accuracy achieved using state-of-the-art
AxO circuits. Specifically, it includes 8 × 8_8 designs from EvoAp-
prox [5] and a hybrid approach that combines AxOSpike’s proposed
AccMSB design with AppAxO’s pruning methodology, referred to
as AppAxO+AccMSB. Fig. 14 presents the corresponding Pareto
fronts with respect to PDP × LUTs utilization and SNN classifi-
cation accuracy. AxOSpike clearly outperforms existing methods,
contributing 93 out of 98 Pareto-optimal designs, while EvoApprox
and AppAxO+AccMSB contribute only 1 and 4 designs, respectively.
These results underscore the value of incorporating application-
specific characteristics into the design of approximate arithmetic
operators.


6
Conclusion
In this article, we presented a comprehensive view of approximate
computing as a multidimensional optimization strategy that ex-
tends beyond energy efficiency. We highlighted recent advances
in AI-guided DSE, surrogate modeling, and application-aware op-
erator design, while also emphasizing the growing importance of
reliability and security co-optimization. While significant progress
has been made, several research challenges remain to unlock the full
potential of approximation. Future directions include explainable
ML and reinforcement learning for intelligent adaptation, integra-
tion with emerging paradigms such as quantum and neuromor-
phic computing, and development of standardized frameworks and
toolchains supporting security, reliability, and accuracy tuning.
Addressing these gaps will cement Approximate Computing as a
foundational pillar in next-generation efficient, safe, and intelligent
systems.

Abstract: The rapid growth of AI workloads is driving interest in Approximate Computing (AxC) as a means to enable low-cost, energy-efficient in- ference in resource-constrained systems. By introducing controlled inaccuracies, AxC can deliver substantial gains in power, perfor- mance, and area (PPA) while leveraging the inherent error tolerance of many AI models. Achieving this potential requires adapting ex- isting frameworks to support the design and optimization of neural networks with approximate operators. Modern AxC research ex- tends beyond accuracy–PPA trade-offs to address reliability and security, reducing redundancy overheads and exploring the distinc- tive side-channel implications of approximation. Application-aware approaches, such as those for spiking neural networks, show that tailoring approximation to workload-specific error behavior can surpass generic strategies. This article examines AI-guided design methods and the interplay between efficiency, reliability, and se- curity, highlighting how these interconnected facets can advance embedded and high-performance computing.
